title: The sugars on a cell's surface aren't frosting — they're the brain's moat
dek: The mucins on the endothelial cells of brain blood vessels are like a redwood forest; with age the leaves fall off and the blood-brain barrier gets leaky. Put the enzyme back with gene therapy and mice remember better.
why: A chemist explains how glycobiology accidentally opened up the blood-brain barrier, with concrete mechanisms and numbers, and the brain shuttle company in the back half is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and investors working on neurodegenerative disease, blood-brain barrier delivery, glycobiology or biologics; researchers interested in how basic science turns into a company.
skip: The first 10 minutes on the history of glycobiology and the M&M analogy — fast-forward to the aging glycome finding at 26:00.

points.h: Glycobiology was abandoned by its tools
points.body: In the 1960s and 70s, carbohydrates were taken as seriously as proteins, but once recombinant DNA arrived, proteins could be cloned, expressed and studied — sugars could not. Sugars are not a product of the central dogma; they are the output of enzymes encoded by hundreds of genes, and molecular biology techniques cannot operate on them directly. So the field rushed toward what could be accelerated, and sugar science, technically hard, was left where it stood. Bertozzi says this is not because sugars are unimportant, but because ‘not studying a field doesn't mean it isn't important.’

points.h: She built the flashlight first, then talked biology
points.body: When she started her lab at Berkeley in 1996, sugar science was missing two things proteins had long had: sequencing (knowing which sugars exist) and live imaging (seeing where sugars are and how they move). Her lab's initial goal was to fill exactly those two holes, and it took about a decade to develop bioorthogonal chemistry — a chemical reaction that can label sugars inside living cells, now a general-purpose tool in the life sciences. Only with a flashlight can you see places no one has looked before.

points.h: No one had asked how sugars change with age
points.body: Tony Wyss-Coray's lab was studying transcriptomic and proteomic changes in brain endothelial cells as they age — standard practice — but no one had asked about the glycome. Sophia, a student who had rotated through Bertozzi's lab, moved to Tony's lab and brought the sugar imaging reagents to compare the brain vasculature of old and young mice. The result was ‘absolutely striking’ — the sugar changes were far more dramatic than any phenotype observed in the transcriptome or proteome.

points.h: Brain endothelial cells have redwood-like mucins
points.body: Mucins sit on the cell surface like giant redwoods: tall, stiff, straight, towering above the other structures. The mucin forest on brain endothelial cells is far thicker than on the blood vessels of heart, kidney or muscle — a landscape unique to the blood-brain barrier. With age this forest turns into winter — leaves gone, trees bare, you can see straight through; young mice are spring, dense with foliage. Sophia found that the enzymes responsible for building these sugars drop in abundance in old mice, and when she restored the enzymes with a gene therapy vector, the mucins recovered, blood-brain barrier leakage fell, and the mice got out of the maze faster.

points.h: A reagent crossed the blood-brain barrier on its own
points.body: Sophia injected a mucin-binding reagent into mice and found hours later that it first bound the vasculature, then crossed the blood-brain barrier by itself into the brain parenchyma. Textbooks say proteins cannot cross the blood-brain barrier alone, and this is the biggest pain point for biologics companies making brain drugs. The accidental finding made the team realize it could serve as a shuttle carrier, delivering cargo into the brain. Sophia now has her own lab at Harvard, and she, Bertozzi, Tony and another student are spinning out a company to do brain shuttling.

More than 150 biologics have been approved to treat immune disease, a similar number for cancer, but only 15 for central nervous system disease — and most of those go in by intrathecal injection: a lumbar puncture, invasive, a whole day gone, hard to scale. If those drugs could be given as ordinary intravenous injections, it would be transformative for patients. The drug types that could get into the brain include monoclonal antibodies, enzyme replacement therapies, siRNA and antisense oligonucleotides, mRNA lipid nanoparticles, and viral and non-viral gene therapy vectors.

points.h: CD22 is the brake on the brain's immune cells
points.body: Tony's lab found that in microglia of aged and Alzheimer's disease mice, the sugar-binding receptor CD22 (Siglec-2) is upregulated. Bertozzi's lab had studied this receptor family in cancer: when they are upregulated they suppress immune cells, letting cancer cells grow unchecked. Microglia are the brain's scavengers, responsible for eating protein aggregates, and their dysfunction is linked to neurodegenerative disease. Blocking CD22 with an antibody made aged mice's microglia more active and their brains cleaner. But at the time there was no brain shuttle, so it could only be injected intracranially — no human therapy possible; now that shuttle technology exists, they can go back and revisit that antibody.

points.h: Today's drugs rest on chemistry from a century ago
points.body: Bioorthogonal chemistry was developed in the early 2000s and is now part of chemists' and biologists' toolkit, with approved drugs that use it. But looking back for her Nobel lecture, Bertozzi found that the underlying chemistry they used to develop these reactions was published in 1915, in 1919, and in 1950 from Germany — all old German-language journals that needed translating. Those chemists could not have foreseen that someone a hundred years later would use it to make cancer drugs. She says most scientists will not know the true impact of their work in their lifetime, and we have to invest in basic science without knowing the impact or the timeline, or the whole pipeline eventually runs dry.

terms.def: A chemical reaction that can be carried out inside living cells without interfering with natural biological processes, used to label and image molecules such as sugars.
The complete set of glycans on a cell's surface, the counterpart to the concepts of genome and proteome.
A heavily glycosylated cell-surface protein, bottlebrush-shaped, forming a thick layer on brain endothelial cells.
An inhibitory receptor that binds sialic acid, suppressing immune cells in cancer and upregulated in microglia with aging.
A molecular carrier that can deliver biologic cargo across the blood-brain barrier into the brain.
